ground_truth.title: VC doesn't work for Climate Tech. Here's 3 new solutions.
ground_truth.author: Manuela Zoninsein
ground_truth.main_content:
A climate hardware founder's field guide to the financing tools that actually work before Series A

Hey there! 👋
Skander here.

You know when you're assembling IKEA furniture, and you're 45 minutes in and you say f* the instruction sheet, I'm doing this myself? And then two hours later you're "done," standing back admiring your work, and you find two screws on the floor that you're absolutely sure weren't there when you started?

That's what financing a climate hardware company feels like. You grind through the fundraising maze (investor meetings, pitch decks, cobbling together enough capital to keep the lights on) only to discover that there were entire categories of financing tools sitting right in front of you the whole time. Tools that could've saved you months of pain and a whole lot of dilution.

The problem is nobody tells you this when you're building physical climate tech. The entire fundraising playbook was written for software companies whose biggest capital expense is AWS credits.

Today, Manuela Zoninsein, founder and CEO of Kadeya, is sharing the map she wished someone had handed her. She spent nearly two years bushwhacking through the financing jungle for her climate hardware startup before the pieces finally clicked. Now she’s drawing the route so you don’t have to.

Today we’re breaking down:

Why the default VC playbook breaks for climate hardware (and why that’s not your fault)

The 3 unconventional financing tools that changed everything for Kadeya

A simple decision tree for founders currently stuck in the valley

Why understanding your capital stack actually makes VCs more interested, not less

🌊 Let’s dive in

But first, who is Manuela?

Manuela Zoninsein is the founder and CEO of Kadeya, a Chicago-based climate tech startup building the world’s first closed-loop beverage refill system. Kadeya’s automated kiosks turn the traditional bottled beverage supply chain into a circular one: dispensing drinks in reusable stainless steel bottles that get returned, sanitized, and refilled on-site, cutting the carbon footprint of a packaged beverage by 75% and eliminating 99.999% of the plastic versus single-use.

The company has piloted with industrial customers including Ecolab and Gilbane Construction, won a contract with the U.S. Air Force, and next month begins commercialization in factories and construction sites across Chicago. Kadeya was recognized with Fast Company’s World Changing Ideas Award.

Before Kadeya, Manuela built companies across three continents. She started her career as a clean tech reporter for Newsweek Magazine and the Engineering News-Record in Beijing, where she lived for eight years and launched her first company, an agtech sales intelligence platform. She then co-founded what became one of the largest online marketplaces for smallholder farmers in Brazil, before moving to Palantir Technologies for international business development and where she helped launch and run a reusable water bottle program along with the company’s kitchen staff. A Brazilian-American fluent in Mandarin, Spanish, and Portuguese, she holds degrees from Harvard, Oxford, and MIT.

Abracadabra: Unlocking the Capital Stack for Climate Tech

Maybe like me, you’ve read a lot about the challenges of early-stage venture investing into hardware and physical climate tech.

Maybe also like me, you walked away thinking: okay, fine, this is gonna be hard… but what am I actually supposed to do?

Most analysis on the capital stack is technically correct but practically useless for early-stage founders. It describes later-stage vehicles, institutional mandates, and idealized trajectories that assume you already survived the messiest, riskiest part.

As a founder, you do not have time to get a Master’s in finance just to translate jargon into action. You are busy building, selling, fixing, shipping, re-building. And raising, lots of raising.

Only recently, as Kadeya started setting up debt instruments, have things finally started to click. It felt like discovering a secret password that unlocks a hidden passageway that’s been in front of me all along, sitting camouflaged along the hedges of a maze I can’t exit.

So in the spirit of helping more people open sesame, without further ado…

1. Kadeya, briefly, and how we funded what many said was impossible

Kadeya builds automated, closed-loop beverage refill systems. We sit at the intersection of hardware, robotics, water, supply chains, and consumer behavior. We also deploy places where people work on their feet with their hands. Which is to say: we are in terrain most investors would rather avoid.

Our early fundraising looked exactly how you’d expect. Angels who’d seen me put my savings on the line for Kadeya. A few brave micro-VCs who put up with my endless haranguing. Lots of small grants plus a few hefty ones thanks to the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program in the federal government, which we accessed through AFWERX (the US Air Force’s innovation arm).

Plus, lots oftrategic believers who understood manufacturing, food systems, climate infrastructure, or who just liked my chutzpah and wanted to see me succeed.

It was a constant exercise in cobbling together capital to keep moving, and planning in weekly budget meetings to see what work could actually get done, when. MacGyvering with what resources we could capture. Stretching every dollar across prototyping, pilots, compliance, talent, all with tariffs and interest rates changing in the background.

2. The capital stack, zoomed out, without the mystique

If you are new to this terrain, start with some great content already shared on Climate Drift. Jarek’s excellent bird’s-eye overview of the capital stack for scaling climate companies is the best on-ramp I’ve seen for understanding what exists, why, for when.

Mairi’s work, particularly on asset-based financing and what she calls the “space laser dilemma,” goes a level deeper. She articulates the structural mismatch between venture expectations and capital-intensive, physical-world innovation far better than I ever could.

Kadeya is now stretching toward accessing asset-based financing (ABF), but what I’m describing today are tools that can be available for other physical tech companies even before ABF becomes an option. Ideally, this means you don’t have to suffer like me and spend ~2 years understanding and building relationships with debt providers, before realizing you are still too early.

If I suffered scraped knees and blistered hands, why must others as well? This isn’t a university sorority where I was hazed, ergo others should be, too. We’re all in this “climate change” thing together, so more people accelerating progress to decarbonization is better for all of us.

Consider it the ultimate network effect.

3. The Valley of Death, defined plainly

People talk about the Valley of Death as if it is a metaphor. It is not.

It is the very real gap between:

Proving your technology works with less-than-necessary resources, and

Reaching scale, predictability, and assets for traditional capital to engage

In this valley, you are too advanced for grants and friends-and-family checks. You are also:

Too risky for banks.
Too capital-intensive for most VCs.
Too early for project finance or customer advances.

Revenue might exist, but it is lumpy.
Assets exist, but they are bespoke.
Risk exists everywhere, not always where investors know how to price it.

You need enough capital that gives you enough visibility to plan, build, and execute a step-change improvement.

This is where most hard tech and climate companies stall or die.

4. Kadeya’s path out of the valley

Here is the part I wish someone had laid out for me earlier. The unconventional yet simple, tried-and-true tools that, together, form a climbable route out of the valley.

Think less “fundraising round” and more Alex Honnold free-soloing his way up Taipei 101. Every move matters. No single tool saves you. What separates the wheat from the chaff? Confidence, focus, time put in training, and stamina.

a. Crowdfunding, seriously

We chose crowdfunding not because it was easy (it’s not), but because it aligns with our stage and the sheer human excitement building around Kadeya’s vision.

Why now:

Community validation matters when markets are being created, not just entered

Customer-investors are patient in ways institutions cannot be

We access optionality without over-optimizing valuation too early

Why Wefunder:

Regulatory clarity

A well-oiled operation that supports non-accredited investors

A growing base of climate-literate (perhaps more accurately, plastic-exhausted) retail backers looking to make the world a bit better (and less congested with disgusting materials none of us ever asked for)

Crowdfunding does not replace institutional capital for us. It complements. Plus it unlocks time, signal, leverage, and an entirely new community of believers who are incentivized to keep Kadeya’s flywheel spinning ever faster.

Crowdfunding was long looked down upon by venture capitalists – maybe because it raised the possibility that all cash is ultimately only a commodity? In this AI-crazed world however, investors who actually care about solving real-world problems are showing appreciation for Kadeya’s creativity, panache, scrappiness, and resilience.

They recognize that we’re in it to win it, and we’re not backing down til we do.

b. Cardinal Robotics and early-stage hard tech debt

This one felt like cheating when we first discovered it.

Cardinal Robotics provides early-stage financing for hard tech companies, backed by major banks, in a way that acknowledges physical assets before traditional lenders will. They call it financing for Robotics-as-a-Service (RaaS), though they lean more toward outright equipment sales or monthly recurring subscriptions / leases.

Their leadership is comprised of roboticists who have themselves built and commercialized physical technologies, before facing financing obstacles. They came to realize this challenge was universal for hardtech and decided to also solve for THAT. They leveraged their legitimacy operating in the trenches to position themselves as early-stage hardware experts to become the outboard asset debt arm for banks who want exposure to physical innovation but don’t have in-house expertise.

Think of Cardinal as a CVC for institutional debt.

Cardinal’s solution matters because:

It decouples progress from equity dilution, which often happens early in the lifecycle of a hardware technology company

It recognizes equipment, tooling, and systems as financeable earlier, and at very competitive interest rates

It bridges the gap between early-stage risk and bank requirements

For us, this was one of the first times the financing system met us where we actually were. It proves the general trend I’m seeing of cool new instruments popping up that employ old-school risk management approaches to solve for this dumb valley of death thing. Let’s avoid making the same mistakes over and over again, right?

For me, it was also one of those a-ha moments where suddenly, the once-fuzzy world snapped into sharp focus and clarity.

c. Supply chain finance, aka factoring

Once you cross roughly $1M in annual order volume, supply chain finance becomes relevant. This would likely follow or complement asset-based financing, but I won’t delve since Mairi already has.

Factoring tools, like those offered by Klear Capital, allow startups to:

Pay suppliers on time

Smooth cash flow without raising more equity

Avoid turning scaleup into a liquidity crisis

And, my personal favorite: accelerate sales cycles with standardized, well-trod paperwork that enterprise CFO’s already know and love

This is not glamorous capital, and perhaps that’s why we don’t hear about it much. It mutes the glitter and allure of venture capital, which might undercut demand for their pricy products. (Microfinance 101: things becomes expensive when supply outstrips demand. That works well for VCs whose jobs are optimizing a high cost of capital.)

With simple math and fiscal discipline, hardtech climate solutions can now be freed to get back to building, generating revenue, and validating scalability. That’s like oxygen during those first moments when you’re rapidly evolving along the crawl-walk-run continuum. It’s like going from toddlerhood, when you kept falling over, to being a 5-year-old who can get real speed. You’ll still make mistakes at this stage, but you are quickly learning what it takes to not bump into those dang corners anymore.

These old-school debt instruments might be the difference between scaling and stalling for physical products. Assume we all agree with the VC Shaun Abrahamson’s “ The Climate Startup Playbook ”, over on Medium, and accept that climate tech is ~2/3 hardware. Could it be, then, that this simple financial tool - which emerged in ~3000 BCE and predates even money and markets - is basically what has stood between today and a decarbonized future?

Or as the Wu-Tang Clan rapped over a decade ago: can it all be so simple?

5. A simple decision tree for founders currently crossing the valley

Here is the mental model I currently use, while layering equity-based venture capital along the way:

Pre-revenue, high uncertainty: grants, angels, crowdfunding

Early, successful pilots, some revenue, low asset base: crowdfunding, micro-VCs, strategic angels and possibly family offices

Recurring revenue plus physical assets: early-stage debt like Cardinal, and after a handful of units are deployed (or so I’m told), you can begin to access asset-based finance

Growing commercial demand, working capital strain: supply chain finance, factoring, working capital loans, and a whole new exciting category that’s taking shape, called FOAK, which Climate Drift has covered in a relatable, tangible fashion, here

Repeatable deployments, predictable cash flows: project finance, traditional debt (I’ve also been hearing about merchant banks for this), growth equity

You do not pick one. You layer them, intentionally and piece by piece, as you mature. And on the right hand column shown below, before you’ve commercialized product, it can be healthy to remain in that iterative loop, improving your model til you can break through to the left hand side of the decision tree.

Most probably, and hopefully, the various instruments complement each other and cover for different aspects of your risk profile at any specific moment (eg: working capital, inventory, payback periods).

That’s what I see as the path, at this point at least. Don’t know yet what happens next but I’m excited to learn! Meanwhile, conversations with VCs are already going more smoothly. Maybe because Kadeya is commercializing, has lots of traction, and can more accurately predict our revenues and margins.

But maybe, just maybe, the conversations are getting easier because I can now say upfront, early and often: we’ve got lower-cost of capital debt to cover for Capex. Boom. Don’t need to spend your expensive equity capital for that heavy physical lifting. Together, we can dedicate your costly cash to focus on growing the business.

Which is exactly what venture capital was designed for.

Closing: stop being SaaS-y

The “secret passageway” is really a mindset shift. You need a willingness to step outside the default venture script and assemble a capital stack that matches reality, not mythology.

It also demands a steep learning curve from Founders/CEOs, who oftentimes are ambitious and bright but who over index on hubris and solipsism.

The two-step required, as always, is: first, self-awareness – i.e,. the ability to recognize when you don’t know something – secondly followed by humility to feel comfortable raising your hand to ask a question, sound stupid, and ask for input and help.

If you are building in climate, hardware, or infrastructure, you are not broken because venture alone does not fit you. The system simply evolved around different assumptions. Assumptions which didn’t consider a world where the most important problem to solve is climate change, and which will be addressed mainly by physical products and infrastructure, not by squishy SaaS-y ones.

Once you understand that, you’ll see the world more clearly and be able to start assessing solutions that won’t waste your time.

And once you start climbing strategically, the valley becomes survivable. I’ve got the calluses and scars to show for it.

Two caveats here:

Family offices take a long time to break into, coming down to chance and the right relationships. Assuming talent is distributed evenly across society, but that capital and networks aren’t, I wouldn’t recommend or rely on this bucket.

There is interesting chatter around topics like “concessionary capital,” “philanthropic investing,” mission-driven investing, “programmatic-related investing,” etc. but I have yet to find a the right puzzle piece that matches Kadeya. Not for lack of trying: I’ve spoken at the conferences with this population and they don’t know how to address infrastructure innovation! So, wouldn’t recommend this, either, at least for now. Stay tuned if I learn more!
